explanations.explanation: Captured, baker. The LORD says to lift up a banner and “…hold nothing back…” (Jeremiah 50:2). You don't raise a banner for small news, either. That's the kind of announcement you make with both hands in the air and a mustache to match.
No crown anywhere in this announcement, friend. The word is that Babylon is captured. A banner going up for a coronation would make sense, but this banner is for a fall.

Forgiveness isn't the headline here. The news the LORD wants announced to the nations is that Babylon is captured (Jeremiah 50:2). Forgiveness does show up later in this passage, but it's for Israel and Judah, not in this announcement.

Not quite, baker, and the text is blunt about it. Bel is put to shame, Marduk is shattered, her images are disgraced and her idols are broken in pieces (Jeremiah 50:2). Bel and Marduk are Babylon's false gods. Nothing in that list comes through in one piece.

Right, they don't make it through. The announcement says Bel is put to shame and Marduk is shattered. Her images are disgraced, and her idols are broken in pieces (Jeremiah 50:2). Bel and Marduk are Babylon's false gods, and the whole list is cracked and crumbled. I've dropped a tray of cookies and I still say that's a gentler landing.

That's it. A nation from the north will come against her and make her land a desolation (Jeremiah 50:3). No one will live in it, and both man and beast will flee. Nobody is left to even turn off the lights.

explanations.answer: A prize split between two kings
explanations.explanation: No splitting of the prize here, baker. The verse says the nation from the north will make her land a desolation. No one will live in it (Jeremiah 50:3). A prize needs somebody left to hand it to.

Bigger would be nice news for Babylon, but that's not what the LORD says. The land becomes a desolation, with no one living in it. Man and beast both flee (Jeremiah 50:3). That's about as far from expansion as you can get.

explanations.answer: The children of Israel and the children of Judah
explanations.explanation: Yes, both of them. The LORD says the children of Israel and the children of Judah will come together, weeping as they come, and will seek the LORD their God (Jeremiah 50:4). Two groups, one direction. That's a long road with a lot of tissues.

The Chaldeans are Babylon's people, and they're the ones this word is against. The ones coming together weeping and seeking the LORD their God are the children of Israel and the children of Judah (Jeremiah 50:4). Different crowd, different road.

explanations.answer: The people of Moab and Edom
explanations.explanation: Moab and Edom aren't named in these verses, friend. The text says it's the children of Israel and the children of Judah who come together, weeping, to seek the LORD their God (Jeremiah 50:4). Keep your eyes on who the verse actually names.

The text says the opposite, baker. They will join themselves to the LORD in “…an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten.” (Jeremiah 50:5). Everlasting means no expiration date. No fine print at the bottom.

Right, this one doesn't run out. They will join themselves to the LORD in “…an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten.” (Jeremiah 50:5). I've lost track of plenty of things in my time, including a whole drawer's worth of years. This covenant will never be forgotten.

Resting place, yes. The LORD says they've wandered from mountain to hill and “…have forgotten their resting place.” (Jeremiah 50:6). They have wandered so long they've lost track of where home even is. Somebody get these folks a chair.

Hiding would sound like they had a plan, friend. The LORD says they “…have forgotten their resting place.” (Jeremiah 50:6). They aren't tucked away somewhere safe. They keep wandering from mountain to hill.
No meeting here, baker. No agenda, no snacks. The verse says they have wandered from mountain to hill and “…have forgotten their resting place.” (Jeremiah 50:6).

explanations.answer: We're not guilty since they sinned against the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's their speech. Their enemies said, “We are not guilty, for they have sinned against the LORD, their true pasture, the LORD, the hope of their fathers.” (Jeremiah 50:7). It's a tidy excuse, but the LORD answers it with a word against Babylon.

explanations.answer: We're not guilty since the LORD gave us their land
explanations.explanation: That's not what they said. Their enemies said, “We are not guilty, for they have sinned against the LORD…” (Jeremiah 50:7). Nothing in their speech mentions being handed any land.

explanations.answer: We're not guilty since our gods told us to do it
explanations.explanation: Their gods don't show up in that speech, friend. The enemies said, “We are not guilty, for they have sinned against the LORD…” (Jeremiah 50:7). The excuse they reached for was about the LORD.

explanations.answer: Flee from the midst of Babylon
explanations.explanation: That's the instruction. The LORD says, “Flee from the midst of Babylon; depart from the land of the Chaldeans…” (Jeremiah 50:8). When the LORD says go, nobody needs to stay behind to fold the napkins.
That's the opposite of what He says. The LORD tells His people to “Flee from the midst of Babylon…” (Jeremiah 50:8). Guard duty on a city that's about to be captured is a rough shift to pick up.

No gift baskets in this passage, baker. The LORD says, “Flee from the midst of Babylon; depart from the land of the Chaldeans…” (Jeremiah 50:8). The only thing He asks them to send is themselves, out the door.

Yes. The LORD says, “For behold, I stir up and bring against Babylon an assembly of great nations from the land of the north.” (Jeremiah 50:9). That's the reason the call to leave comes first. Staying put in a place with that coming is a hard plan to defend.

This one is true, friend. The LORD says, “For behold, I stir up and bring against Babylon an assembly of great nations from the land of the north.” (Jeremiah 50:9). The call to leave comes right after that.

Not so, baker. The LORD says, “Chaldea will be plundered; all who plunder her will have their fill…” (Jeremiah 50:10). Having your fill means they don't leave hungry for more. Barely anything isn't in that verse.
Right, they leave full. The LORD says, “Chaldea will be plundered; all who plunder her will have their fill…” (Jeremiah 50:10). Nobody walks away with an empty box here.

Least, yes. The LORD says, “Behold, she will be the least of the nations, a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert.” (Jeremiah 50:12). Her mother will be greatly ashamed too. That's a long fall from the loud celebration just before it.

Envy would mean everybody wants what she has, friend. The LORD says the opposite: “Behold, she will be the least of the nations, a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert.” (Jeremiah 50:12). Nobody is jealous of a desert.
Pride is what the celebrating looked like, baker. But the LORD says her mother will be greatly ashamed and “…she will be the least of the nations…” (Jeremiah 50:12). The shame takes pride's seat.
No sightseeing here, friend. The text says, “All who pass through Babylon will be horrified and will hiss at all her wounds.” (Jeremiah 50:13). Nobody stops for a photo. They are horrified.

Right, nobody stops to admire. Because of the wrath of the LORD, she will not be inhabited and will become completely desolate. “All who pass through Babylon will be horrified and will hiss at all her wounds.” (Jeremiah 50:13). The people walking through don't linger to take in the view.

explanations.answer: She has sinned against the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the LORD gives. He says, “Shoot at her! Spare no arrows! For she has sinned against the LORD.” (Jeremiah 50:14). The text gives one reason, and it's that one.

explanations.answer: She has run low on soldiers
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say a thing about her soldiers, baker. The reason given is “For she has sinned against the LORD.” (Jeremiah 50:14). Her troop count isn't the point here.
No kings are insulted in that verse, friend. The LORD says, “Spare no arrows! For she has sinned against the LORD.” (Jeremiah 50:14). His reason is the one on the page.

explanations.answer: Thrown up her hands in surrender
explanations.explanation: Hands up. The text says, “She has thrown up her hands in surrender; her towers have fallen; her walls are torn down.” (Jeremiah 50:15). The war cry is still going while she's already giving up.

explanations.answer: Called on her allies for help
explanations.explanation: No phone calls to allies in this verse, baker. It says, “She has thrown up her hands in surrender…” (Jeremiah 50:15). Nobody is coming to help her.

explanations.answer: Fired back from her high towers
explanations.explanation: Her towers aren't firing back, friend. The verse says her towers have fallen and her walls are torn down. “She has thrown up her hands in surrender…” (Jeremiah 50:15). It's hard to shoot from a tower that's already on the ground.
Same, yes. “Since this is the vengeance of the LORD, take out your vengeance upon her; as she has done, do the same to her.” (Jeremiah 50:15). What she did comes back to her in the same shape.
Opposite would mean she gets treated kindly, baker. The verse says, “…as she has done, do the same to her.” (Jeremiah 50:15). It's the same, not the opposite.
No bare minimum in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “…as she has done, do the same to her.” (Jeremiah 50:15). The measure is what she has done.

Yes, that's what the text says. The LORD says, “In the face of the oppressor's sword, each will turn to his own people, each will flee to his own land.” (Jeremiah 50:16). Everybody heads for home. I know that feeling of wanting to head home, believe me.

This one is true, baker. After the sower and the one who wields the sickle are cut off, the LORD says, “In the face of the oppressor's sword, each will turn to his own people, each will flee to his own land.” (Jeremiah 50:16). Each one heads back to his own people.

Assyria's king, yes. The LORD says, “The first to devour him was the king of Assyria; the last to crush his bones was Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.” (Jeremiah 50:17). Nebuchadnezzar is the king of Babylon, and he's named last.
Persia isn't named in that verse, friend. The first to devour Israel is “…the king of Assyria…” (Jeremiah 50:17). Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, is the last named.
Tyre doesn't show up in this picture, baker. The LORD says, “The first to devour him was the king of Assyria…” (Jeremiah 50:17). Then Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon comes last.

It is. The LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says, “I will punish the king of Babylon and his land as I punished the king of Assyria.” (Jeremiah 50:18). The LORD names the Assyrian king in the same breath. Babylon's king isn't getting a different rulebook.
This one is true, friend. The LORD says, “I will punish the king of Babylon and his land as I punished the king of Assyria.” (Jeremiah 50:18). He ties the two kings together in one sentence.

Satisfied, yes. The LORD says, “I will return Israel to his pasture, and he will graze on Carmel and Bashan; his soul will be satisfied on the hills of Ephraim and Gilead.” (Jeremiah 50:19). Think of the feeling when you finally sit down after a long shift on your feet, only bigger.
No fear in this verse, baker. The LORD says Israel's soul “…will be satisfied on the hills of Ephraim and Gilead.” (Jeremiah 50:19). He's brought home, so the fear isn't in the picture.
Restless is how the wandering sounded, friend. But the LORD says that back home, “…his soul will be satisfied on the hills of Ephraim and Gilead.” (Jeremiah 50:19). The wandering has ended.
None. The LORD says, “…a search will be made for Israel's guilt, but there will be none…” (Jeremiah 50:20). Somebody goes looking and comes back empty-handed, which is the best kind of empty.
Plenty would be a hard word to hear, baker. But the LORD says a search will be made for Israel's guilt, “…but there will be none…” (Jeremiah 50:20). The search turns up nothing.

Not even some, friend. The LORD says, “…a search will be made for Israel's guilt, but there will be none…” (Jeremiah 50:20). He also says, “…for I will forgive the remnant I preserve.” (Jeremiah 50:20).
